doc.title: Pete Barbutti interviewed by Monk Rowe, via Zoom, December 8, 2022

chapter: Vegas groups and Spokane solo years
title: First solo gig at the Stockyards Inn, Spokane
summary: Getting to Spokane on a ticket from agent John Powell and the absurd room owned by Rocky Rothrock: bar, bulb, mirror, microphone.

story.theme_name: Coming to New York: clubs, jams, and making it
story.community_name: Making it in New York: arrival, clubs and the scene

blocks.x: and for some reason it popped into my head. But George Burke set it up and it was my first single ever and so I was terrified. And I said, “George I’m ashamed to tell you I don’t have the money to get to Spokane and I don’t have a car.” So he said, “Well take the bus.” I said, “Okay but it takes like a day and a half to get there on the bus.” It stopped everywhere, you know, Fresno and Elko, and so George Burke said, “Okay I’ll send you a money order.” This was before you could transfer money. And so I said, “Okay but I need it by” whatever — like Thursday if I’m going to get to Spokane for Saturday. He says, “Don’t worry about it.” Anyway it didn’t get there and I called him and said, “Look, I never got the money and the bus is leaving in five minutes and I can’t get on it.” And George just washed his hands of everything — this is to another agent in Spokane, a guy named John Powell. He lives up there, and I don’t know, just call him. So I called John Powell and John said you know, “They’re advertising you and everything, direct from Las Vegas.” So I said — so he said, “I’ll send you an airline ticket.” You could wire it in those days. So he sent me an airline ticket and the pay was $300 a week and the airline ticket was $309. So before I got on the plane I was out $9. Anyway I got the ticket, I flew to Spokane, and I had on one of the suits from the band and a very hip topcoat and a goatee. And John Powell looked at me and I looked like an alien. I mean Spokane is really conservative, right wing. And he looked at me and he said, “This isn’t a jazz gig you know.” I said, “Well I know, John, I’ll do the best I can.” So we drove out, it was February and it was pouring rain. And we drove out — my youngest son was just born a few weeks before this. So we drove out to the club and there was a big sign on the club. It said, “Direct from Las Vegas” and he misspelled Las Vegas, he had L-O-S. And then I realized why it’s called The Stockyards Inn, it was in the middle of the stockyards, so we had to walk on planks across the steer poop to get to the club. And the guy’s name who owned it was — his dad was very rich and this guy wanted to have a club so his dad said here, here’s some money. His name was Rocky Rothrock. And I went in and the room was okay, it was a rectangular room, a decent size, and he said, “Well what do you need?” I said, “Well the best thing would be a piano bar.” Well you mention a piano bar to most people today they sort of know what you’re talking about. But Rocky, you know, from another planet somehow. He said, “What’s that?” I said, “Well it’s like you’ve got a bar, the piano, it’s like a bar and the people can sit and talk to you and drink while you’re playing requests.” And he said, “Oh that’s a good idea. I got you covered.” So I went into work that night and he had an old upright piano up against the wall and he built a bar around the back of me. So the people were looking at the back of my head and the piano was almost unplayable and so I did the best I could. And then after a couple of nights more and more people started to come into the bar and I said, “Rocky you know it’d help if there was a light in the corner of that room you know.” He said, “Okay.” So I went in © Fillius Jazz Archive -11-

the next night and I’m not exaggerating, he had a cord hanging down from the ceiling and a 100 watt bulb with like a poolroom shade over it.” And I’d go [scats] and turn on the light and everybody’d go whoa [shields eyes] you know it was dark in the room. And then I said, Rocky, with this piano like this I can’t see the people.” So the next invention of his was on top of the piano he mounted a mirror from a dresser and it would swivel. And he gave me a dowel so I could reach up and move the mirror. My final request was if I could get a microphone. He said, “Well we’ve got a sound system in the whole building,” he said, “that’s no big deal, I’ll get you a microphone.” So he got me one of those little microphones like Broderick Crawford in “Highway Patrol” you know, Broderick Crawford, where you’d squeeze the thing and talk into it. And I’d set it on the edge of the piano just where the keyboard ends, I’d set it there. And then I’d pick it up and I’d turn to the audience and I was doing jokes and I was doing local stuff and people started to come in, the place was getting crowded and everything. And then the crowning blow was I was right in the middle of a story one night and over the same speakers that my voice is emanating I hear, “Johnson party of six, two chicken fried steaks, two fried chicken.” It was like it was hooked up to the cook and everything. So I started yelling at this guy who was the manager. His name was Mr. McClusky. And even his son called him Mr. McClusky, he was that revered as a restaurant manager in Spokane. So I deleted the “Mr.” it was blasphemy. I called him “McClusky” and then boy people were going oh my God he called him McClusky, it was like a big sin. Anyway I carried on.
